message.content: {"findings":"The claim looks like a misreading of a study. The 30% figure comes from a UC Berkeley Center for Studies in Higher Education working paper by Igor Chirikov. That paper analyzed a large Texas research university, not UC Berkeley. It found that the share of A grades in AI-exposed courses rose 13 percentage points, about 30% relative to the 2022 baseline (https://cshe.berkeley.edu/publications/artificial-intelligence-and-grade-inflation-cshe-higher-education-working-paper-series). Coverage that says Berkeley found a 30% rise confuses the study's author affiliation with the school it studied (https://www.capitalaidaily.com/uc-berkeley-study-of-500000-grades-finds-ai-inflated-a-grades-by-30-but-student-learning-remains-questionable/). The Daily Californian's Berkeleytime data shows A's at UC Berkeley stayed between 30% and 35% from 2019 to spring 2026, so it found no comparable increase (https://www.dailycal.org/news/campus/academics/uc-berkeley-shows-no-signs-of-ai-grade-inflation-as-professors-adapt/article_6da85b38-889f-4f80-835a-88cc54a81662.html). Berkeley's own long-term grade inflation was real but smaller. A's and A-minuses rose from about 50% of grades in 2013 to 64% in 2022, which is 13 percentage points, or roughly 26% in relative terms (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2023/uc-berkeley-grade-inflation/ and https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/grade-inflation-must-no-substitute-020358502.html). That combined A/A- figure is not the same as A grades alone, and it covers a decade rather than the AI period. So the claim that A's at UC Berkeley are up 30% is not supported as stated.","correction_needed":true}

{"findings":"The claim looks like a misattribution. The 30% figure comes from a UC Berkeley CSHE working paper by Igor Chirikov. That paper studied a large research university in Texas, not UC Berkeley. It found that the share of A grades in AI-exposed courses rose by 13 percentage points, about 30% relative to the 2022 baseline (https://cshe.berkeley.edu/publications/artificial-intelligence-and-grade-inflation-cshe-higher-education-working-paper-series, https://www.capitalaidaily.com/uc-berkeley-study-of-500000-grades-finds-ai-inflated-a-grades-by-30-but-student-learning-remains-questionable/). The paper was written at Berkeley, but its data is not from Berkeley grades.

The Daily Californian found that A's at UC Berkeley stayed between 30% and 35% from 2019 to spring 2026. It found no equivalent AI-driven trend there (https://www.dailycal.org/news/campus/academics/uc-berkeley-shows-no-signs-of-ai-grade-inflation-as-professors-adapt/article_6da85b38-889f-4f80-835a-88cc54a81662.html).

The SF Chronicle reports a different set of figures. About 64% of Berkeley undergraduate grades were A's or A-minuses in 2022, up 13 percentage points from 10 years earlier (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2023/uc-berkeley-grade-inflation/). That is roughly a 25% relative rise over a decade, from about 51% to 64%. It includes A-minuses, and it is not the 30% figure the article cites. The Daily Cal series and the SF Chronicle series count different things, so the two sources don't directly conflict.

Berkeley's own A's have not risen 30% in the AI-era sense the claim implies. The 30% number belongs to the Texas study.","correction_needed":true}
